description: Somos uma equipe apaixonada por dados de satélite e pela proteção ambiental. Nosso projeto busca harmonizar os focos de calor detectados pelos sensores MODIS e VIIRS da NASA, corrigindo diferenças de resolução e horário de passagem para gerar um mapa único e confiável de queimadas.
summary: Flaming View turns 23 years of NASA heat-detection data into a single, comparable record for the entire world. NASA FIRMS combines different sensors (MODIS since 2003, VIIRS S-NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018) with different resolutions, which makes it impossible to compare distant time periods. Our pipeline harmonizes these sensors into 0.05° monthly cells, using conversion factors that are calibrated and validated out of sample, and it reports the uncertainty for each converted year. On top of this foundation, a machine learning model that uses fire history estimates risk for the next 1 to 3 months, by territory. Our evaluation measures whether the forecast beats the historical average for the same time of year: in a preliminary test with INPE data, even a simple model reduced error by about 30% in 2024 and 2025, both extreme years. The data is published in versioned releases with checksums, and a web interface shows the seasonality of fire. The project helps anticipate the fire season and plan brigade deployment, and it uses only open data.
details:
Flaming View is a decision-support platform for wildfire prevention, built for the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge with a focus on Brazil. NASA detects fire hot spots from space with two sensors: MODIS, in operation since 2000, and VIIRS, in operation since 2012. Because VIIRS has a higher resolution, it records about four times as many hot spots over the same area. As a result, comparing the years before and after 2012 without correction shows an increase in fire that partly never happened. The problem became more urgent on November 2, 2026, when the S-NPP satellite stopped delivering data.

To solve this, we downloaded FIRMS hot spots from 2003 to 2025. We counted each square of about 1 km only once per day and never added the two sensors together in the same year, which prevents the same fire from being counted twice. Using the years when both sensors operated together, 2013 to 2019, we calculated a conversion factor for each 2° × 2° region and each month of the year. We tested this factor on 2020 and 2021, years left out of the calculation, and obtained a 4.7% error in the monthly total and an R² of 0.96. We also excluded Aqua satellite data after 2021, because its orbital drift changed its overpass time and increased detections without any real increase in fire. The result is a consistent 23-year record, which continues with the NOAA-20 satellite after the end of S-NPP.

On top of this record, a Random Forest model forecasts, for the next 1 to 3 months, the risk class of each area (low, normal, high, or critical) relative to that area's own history. The model uses past hot spots, NOAA's El Niño index, and NASA POWER anomalies of rainfall, temperature, humidity, and wind. It was trained on data up to 2022 and tested on 2023, 2024, and 2025. In testing, the AUC was 0.71 for the following month. Among the 10% of areas the model ranked as highest risk, 33.8% had a critical fire month, compared with 13.8% across all areas, or 2.4 times more.

Next, the Preventive Priority Index combines the forecast, weighted at 50%, fire history, at 25%, and exposure, at 25%. Exposure considers IBGE population density and FUNAI Indigenous Lands. The three scores are multiplied rather than added, so an area only reaches the top if it is critical in all three dimensions. Eight fixed rules turn this result into preventive actions, such as pre-positioning fire brigades, coordinating with FUNAI, and suspending controlled-burn permits, and the manager accepts or dismisses each one. An AI assistant explains each area's data and drafts the report, but it makes no decisions. Without the AI, the system keeps working with the rule texts.

The main benefit is lead time. Current tools show where fire is burning now or indicate the risk for the next few days. Flaming View shows where fire is likely to be strongest in the coming months, which is the time needed to hire brigades, build firebreaks, and plan budgets. The intended impact is that civil defense and environmental agencies can use the same effort to reach the highest-risk areas, with special attention to Indigenous peoples and exposed populations. All data are public and free, and the harmonization and forecast work worldwide.

We used data from NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER, NOAA, IBGE, and FUNAI, obtained through INPE's TerraBrasilis. Data processing and modeling were done in Python with pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Parquet, scikit-learn, and H3. The back end uses FastAPI and the Anthropic API (Claude) for the assistant. The front end uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, GSAP, and Lenis, with an interface in Portuguese and English. The demo video was produced with Playwright and Remotion. Parts of the code were generated with the help of Claude, based on a requirements document written by the team.

The creative aspect is using harmonization, the challenge itself, as the foundation of a prevention product rather than an end in itself: the system takes satellite data all the way to an action plan on a single screen, designed to look like a public geospatial intelligence system. The team prioritized reliability, measuring every metric on years the model had not seen and reporting the accuracy of each forecast horizon separately. The 1-month forecast is solid, while the 2- and 3-month forecasts indicate trends. We also prioritized transparency, since the AI explains but does not decide, the inclusion of Indigenous Lands in the priority calculation, and low maintenance cost, with open data and automatic monthly updates. We acknowledge as limitations that vegetation is not yet part of the model, that population is measured at the municipal level, and that validation with civil defense agencies is the next step.
